title: How the Silk Road Actually Worked (and What Could Go Terribly Wrong On It)
description: You don’t have to spend a long time read­ing up on the Silk Road before you see the term itself (“Silk Road”) called a mis­nomer. In fact, wh
body:
You don’t have to spend a long time read­ing up on the Silk Road before you see the term itself (“Silk Road”) called a mis­nomer. In fact, what we refer to by that name com­pris­es a whole net­work of trade routes con­nect­ing Asia, Africa, and Europe, whose traf­fic con­stant­ly shift­ed over a mil­len­ni­um and a half accord­ing to cli­mat­ic, geopo­lit­i­cal, and civ­i­liza­tion­al con­di­tions. Nor was silk the only, or even the pri­ma­ry type of good car­ried along those routes. From East to West went tea, dyes, per­fumes, porce­lain, and paper; from West to East, glass­ware, hors­es, camels, hon­ey, wine, and gold, to name just a few items in peren­ni­al demand. It was along the Silk Road, or Silk-and-Many-Oth­er-Things-Roads, that gun­pow­der spread out of Chi­na — and the Black Death spread out of Europe.
Accord­ing to the Knowl­ed­gia video above, the rough­ly 4,000-mile-long Silk Road was offi­cial­ly opened in 130 BC. But it was­n’t with­out its pre­de­ces­sors: in 500 BC, for exam­ple, the “Roy­al Road” estab­lished by Dar­ius I’s Achaemenid Empire “stretched from Susa, which lies in mod­ern-day Iran, all the way, near­ly 2,000 miles to the west, to Sardis, which is today a part of Turkey,” with spurs reach­ing India and North­ern Africa.
What­ev­er its eco­nom­ic impact, the Roy­al Road had noth­ing like the cul­tur­al effects of the Silk Road, any his­to­ry of which empha­sizes the “new think­ing and new ways of life being passed along the net­work of trade routes,” to say noth­ing of “the spread of reli­gions or ide­olo­gies that would occur thanks to the mer­chants and trav­el­ers them­selves.”


	

This despite the fact that few of those mer­chants or trav­el­ers crossed the Silk Road­’s entire length. But we can all name at least one man who made the full jour­ney: the thir­teenth-cen­tu­ry Venet­ian explor­er Mar­co Polo, who as a teenag­er first made the trek to Kublai Khan’s plea­sure dome with his father. (At that point, the Mon­gol Empire had already uni­fied its routes, but not before lay­ing waste to a fair few set­tle­ments along the way.) It is to Polo’s writ­ings that we owe our endur­ing­ly roman­tic image of the Silk Road, but he under­stood the dan­gers of that law­less gaunt­let across empires as well as any­one. The Urban Atlas video above lists a few of them, includ­ing desert heat, dis­eases, hal­lu­ci­na­tions, ban­dit­ry, and slav­ery. Today, we encounter no such per­ils on the way from Rome to Xi’an, a jour­ney we can make on a flight with a stopover in Bei­jing. Per­haps Mar­co Polo would say we’ve all gone soft, but then, he’d prob­a­bly be more inter­est­ed in learn­ing about our roads in the sky.

title: The Radical Ideas of Plato’s Republic: An In-Depth Introduction
description:
in Philosophy, Politics |   	September 15th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

We no longer live in a time when col­lege fresh­men get shocked by much
body:
in Philosophy, Politics |   	September 15th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

We no longer live in a time when col­lege fresh­men get shocked by much of the read­ing mate­r­i­al assigned to them. Coun­ter­in­tu­itive­ly, the texts that do retain their pow­er to dis­turb young minds (pre­sum­ing they can read texts in the first place) tend to skew old — and in one promi­nent case, about 2,400 years old. Even the most super­fi­cial inter­pre­ta­tions of Pla­to’s Repub­lic chal­lenge the polit­i­cal assump­tions held by almost every stu­dent today, at least in the devel­oped West. Many of them hold those assump­tions so deeply that they’ve nev­er artic­u­lat­ed them. Encoun­ter­ing the argu­ments made by Pla­to’s Socrates in favor of a soci­ety ruled by an enlight­ened upper class, tight­ly con­trolled from above in every­thing from the divi­sion of its labor to the con­tent of its art, prompts them to do so. 
Or rather, it prompts them to do so in an ide­al edu­ca­tion­al set­ting, but then, Pla­to was ded­i­cat­ed to noth­ing so much as the ide­al. When he casts Socrates as mak­ing the case for the best pos­si­ble rela­tion­ships between ruler, state, and indi­vid­ual, he cre­ates less a how-to man­u­al (as Machi­avel­li did nine­teen cen­turies lat­er, in a bru­tal­ly qua­si-satir­i­cal spir­it) than a means of bet­ter under­stand­ing extant soci­eties by bring­ing their char­ac­ter­is­tics into relief through com­par­i­son.
We may reflex­ive­ly quote Churchill’s remark about mod­ern democ­ra­cy, vul­ner­a­ble as it is to manip­u­la­tion by all man­ner of unsa­vory actors, being “the worst form of Gov­ern­ment except for all those oth­er forms that have been tried from time to time,” but we nev­er­the­less flinch from hold­ing it up too close­ly against any kind of ide­al sys­tem.
It’s tempt­ing to declare that we would­n’t want to live in the repub­lic of the Repub­lic. (Some of us may have suc­cumbed to that temp­ta­tion in the polit­i­cal-phi­los­o­phy lec­ture hall.) But a more reflec­tive read­ing reveals a good deal about Pla­to’s time as well as our own. In the 78-minute video above, Jared Hen­der­son takes us through the Socrat­ic dia­logues that pro­pose and refine this Utopia, with its philoso­pher-kings, noble lies, spir­i­tu­al aris­to­crats, breed­ing fes­ti­vals, and guardians trained from the cra­dle. He arrives at cer­tain unfash­ion­able ideas, such as the ulti­mate task of refin­ing one’s own soul and the neces­si­ty of per­suad­ing those imper­vi­ous to phi­los­o­phy with myth. Even those of us who regard our­selves as sophis­ti­cat­ed thinkers, imper­vi­ous to the crude rhetoric of ide­olo­gies and dem­a­gogues, would do well to ask our­selves: how much of that think­ing has been shaped by the sto­ries we’ve heard all our lives?

title: How Martin Luther King, Jr. Used Nietzsche, Hegel & Kant to Overturn Segregation in America
description:
Image by Dick DeMar­si­co, via Wiki­me­dia Com­mons
The influ­ence of Georg Wil­helm Friedrich Hegel on the rev­o­lu­tion­ary phi­los­o­phy of Ka
body:
Image by Dick DeMar­si­co, via Wiki­me­dia Com­mons
The influ­ence of Georg Wil­helm Friedrich Hegel on the rev­o­lu­tion­ary phi­los­o­phy of Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels is well known. Marx wrote a cri­tique of Hegel’s Phi­los­o­phy of Right and claimed to have turned the Ger­man ide­al­ist philoso­pher on his head, and the devel­op­ment of Marx­ist the­o­ry among a school of neo-Hegelians, wrote Rebec­ca Coop­er in 1925, occurred in a peri­od “pecu­liar­ly aus­pi­cious for the birth of a rev­o­lu­tion­ary social phi­los­o­phy.”
A cen­tu­ry lat­er, on anoth­er con­ti­nent, Hegel’s thought influ­enced the course of a very dif­fer­ent strug­gle. And while the his­tor­i­cal con­di­tions of mid-nine­teenth-cen­tu­ry Europe and mid-twen­ti­eth-cen­tu­ry Amer­i­ca present entire­ly dif­fer­ent sets of spe­cif­ic con­cerns, the same gen­er­al obser­va­tion applies: the time and place of such rad­i­cal thinkers as Mal­colm X, Angela Davis, Huey New­ton and a host of oth­er activists pre­sent­ed “pecu­liar­ly aus­pi­cious” cir­cum­stances for rev­o­lu­tion­ary social phi­los­o­phy.
But while these fig­ures appear today as the van­guard of rad­i­cal black thought, Mar­tin Luther King, Jr., the most wide­ly cel­e­brat­ed of Civ­il Rights lead­ers, “is often con­flat­ed with neolib­er­al mul­ti­cul­tur­al­ism,” writes Crit­i­cal The­o­ry, his pro­gram asso­ci­at­ed with “the fail­ure of the civ­il rights move­ment to dis­man­tle the ongo­ing sys­temic white suprema­cy of the sta­tus quo.” And yet, King’s move­ment not only suc­ceed­ed in end­ing legal seg­re­ga­tion and has­ten­ing the pass­ing of the Civ­il Rights Act; it also pro­vid­ed direc­tion for near­ly every non­vi­o­lent social move­ment from his day to ours. King’s lega­cy is not only that of an inspir­ing orga­niz­er and ora­tor, but also of a rad­i­cal thinker who engaged crit­i­cal­ly with phi­los­o­phy and social the­o­ry and brought it to bear on his activism.
We are gen­er­al­ly well aware of King’s debt to Gand­hi and the Satya­gra­ha move­ment that won Indi­an inde­pen­dence in 1947, yet we know lit­tle of his debt to the same thinker who inspired Marx and his contemporaries—G.W.F. Hegel. As philoso­pher Nolen Gertz has demon­strat­ed on his blog, King was high­ly influ­enced by Hegelian­ism, as much as, or per­haps even more so, than he was by Gand­hi’s move­ment. Marx may have turned Hegel’s sys­tem on its head, but King, writes Gertz, “fought White Amer­i­ca… by turn­ing the ideas of dead white men against the oppres­sive prac­tices of liv­ing white men.”

King read and wrote on Hegel as a grad­u­ate stu­dent at Boston Uni­ver­si­ty and Har­vard in the mid-’50s, where he stud­ied the­ol­o­gy and the his­to­ry of phi­los­o­phy and reli­gion. He took a year­long sem­i­nar on Hegel with his advi­sor at BU, Edgar Bright­man (see King’s dia­gram notes of Hegel’s sys­tem above), and found a great deal to admire in the “dead white” philosopher’s log­i­cal sys­tem, as well as a good deal to cri­tique. The two-semes­ter class, King wrote in his auto­bi­og­ra­phy, was “both reward­ing and stim­u­lat­ing”:
Although the course was main­ly a study of Hegel’s mon­u­men­tal work, Phe­nom­e­nol­o­gy of Mind, I spent my spare time read­ing his Phi­los­o­phy of His­to­ry and Phi­los­o­phy of Right. There were points in Hegel’s phi­los­o­phy that I strong­ly dis­agreed with. For instance, his absolute ide­al­ism was ratio­nal­ly unsound to me because it tend­ed to swal­low up the many in the one. But there were oth­er aspects of his think­ing that I found stim­u­lat­ing. His con­tention that “truth is the whole” led me to a philo­soph­i­cal method of ratio­nal coher­ence. His analy­sis of the dialec­ti­cal process, in spite of its short­com­ings, helped me to see that growth comes through strug­gle.
While King may have dis­agreed with Hegel’s ide­al­ism, he found sup­port for his own phi­los­o­phy of non­vi­o­lence in Hegel’s dialec­ti­cal method, a mode of analy­sis that seems par­tic­u­lar­ly well suit­ed to social­ly rev­o­lu­tion­ary thought. In Stride Toward Free­dom, King wrote,
The third way open to oppressed peo­ple in their quest for free­dom is the way of non­vi­o­lent resis­tance. Like the syn­the­sis in Hegelian phi­los­o­phy, the prin­ci­ple of non­vi­o­lent resis­tance seeks to rec­on­cile the truths of two opposites—acquiescence and violence—while avoid­ing the extremes and immoral­i­ties of both.
King’s crit­i­cal appraisal of Hegel extend­ed to oth­er rad­i­cal philo­soph­i­cal thinkers as well, includ­ing Kant, Spin­oza, Kierkegaard, Marx, and Niet­zsche. Gertz offers many sam­ples of the bud­ding Civ­il Rights leader’s notes on var­i­ous thinkers and philoso­phies, includ­ing the first para­graph of an essay enti­tled “Pil­grim­age to Non­vi­o­lence” (below), in which King con­fess­es that his encounter with Exis­ten­tial­ism often “shocked” him, espe­cial­ly since he had “been raised in a rather strict fun­da­men­tal­ist tra­di­tion.” And yet, he writes—in an allu­sion to Kant’s reac­tion to David Hume—he acquired “a new appre­ci­a­tion for objec­tive appraisal and crit­i­cal analy­sis” that “knocked me out of my dog­mat­ic slum­ber.”

In the essay, King writes, “I became con­vinced that exis­ten­tial­ism, in spite of the fact that it had become all too fash­ion­able, had grasped cer­tain basic truths about man.” He seems par­tic­u­lar­ly drawn to Kierkegaard (see his notes on the philoso­pher below). Yet it is Hegel who seems most respon­si­ble for awak­en­ing his philo­soph­i­cal curios­i­ty. As King schol­ar John Ans­bro dis­cov­ered, King “stat­ed in a Jan­u­ary 19, 1956 inter­view with The Mont­gomery Adver­tis­er that Hegel was his favorite philoso­pher.” Lat­er that year, King gave an address to the First Annu­al Insti­tute on Non­vi­o­lence and Social Change in which he used Hegelian terms to char­ac­ter­ize the Civ­il Rights strug­gle: “Long ago, the Greek philoso­pher Her­a­cli­tus argued that jus­tice emerges from the strife of oppo­sites, and Hegel, in mod­ern phi­los­o­phy, preached a doc­trine of growth through strug­gle.”

Inde­pen­dent schol­ar Ralph Dumain has fur­ther cat­a­logued King’s many approv­ing ref­er­ences to Hegel, includ­ing a paper he wrote enti­tled “An Expo­si­tion of the First Tri­ad of Cat­e­gories of the Hegelian Logic—Being, Non-Being, Becom­ing,” the “last of six essays that King wrote” for his two-semes­ter course on the philoso­pher. King also approached Hegel by way of an ear­li­er Civ­il Rights leader—W.E.B. Du Bois, who read the Ger­man philoso­pher while study­ing with promi­nent social sci­en­tists in Berlin, and who applied Hegelian log­ic to his own analy­sis of racial con­scious­ness and strug­gle in Amer­i­ca.
Inter­est­ing­ly, what nei­ther King nor Du Bois remarked on is the fact that Hegel was like­ly him­self inspired by black rev­o­lu­tion­ar­ies. The Hait­ian Rev­o­lu­tion, argues schol­ar Susan Buck-Morss, gave Hegel the impe­tus for his analy­sis of pow­er and his “metaphor of the ‘strug­gle to death’ between the mas­ter and slave, which for Hegel pro­vid­ed the key to the unfold­ing of free­dom in world his­to­ry.” While Hegel’s thought is a philo­soph­i­cal thread that winds through the work of rad­i­cal thinkers through­out the nine­teenth and twen­ti­eth cen­turies, his own phi­los­o­phy may not have tak­en the direc­tion it did with­out the rev­o­lu­tion­ary strug­gles against oppres­sion waged by for­mer slaves in the New World cen­turies before King led his non­vi­o­lent war on the oppres­sive sys­tem of seg­re­ga­tion in the Unit­ed States.
H/T Nolen Gertz
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2015.

title: Why Incompetent People Think They’re Amazing: An Animated Lesson from David Dunning (of the Famous  “Dunning-Kruger Effect”)
description:
in Business, Psychology, TED Talks |   	September 15th, 2026  1 Comment
	
			

	

The busi­ness world has long had spe­cial jar­gon for the Kafkaesq
body:
in Business, Psychology, TED Talks |   	September 15th, 2026  1 Comment
	
			

	

The busi­ness world has long had spe­cial jar­gon for the Kafkaesque incom­pe­tence bedev­il­ing the ranks of upper man­age­ment. There is “the Peter prin­ci­ple,” first described in a satir­i­cal book of the same name in 1968. More recent­ly, we have the pos­i­tive notion of “fail­ing upward.” The con­cept has inspired a mantra, “fail hard­er, fail faster,” as well as pop­u­lar books like The Gift of Fail­ure. Famed research pro­fes­sor, author, and TED talk­er Brené Brown has called TED “the fail­ure con­fer­ence,” and indeed, a “Fail­Con” does exist, “in over a dozen cities on 6 con­ti­nents around the globe.”
The can­dor about this most unavoid­able of human phe­nom­e­na may prove a boon to pub­lic health, low­er­ing lev­els of hyper­ten­sion by a sig­nif­i­cant mar­gin. But is there a dan­ger in prais­ing fail­ure too fer­vent­ly? (Samuel Beckett’s quote on the mat­ter, beloved by many a 21st-cen­tu­ry thought leader, proves decid­ed­ly more ambigu­ous in con­text.) Might it present an even greater oppor­tu­ni­ty for peo­ple to “rise to their lev­el of incom­pe­tence”? Giv­en the preva­lence of the “Dun­ning-Kruger Effect,” a cog­ni­tive bias explained by John Cleese in a pre­vi­ous post, we may not be well-placed to know whether our efforts con­sti­tute suc­cess or fail­ure, or whether we actu­al­ly have the skills we think we do.
First described by social psy­chol­o­gists David Dun­ning (Uni­ver­si­ty of Michi­gan) and Justin Kruger (N.Y.U.) in 1999, the effect “sug­gests that we’re not very good at eval­u­at­ing our­selves accu­rate­ly.” So says the nar­ra­tor of the TED-Ed les­son above, script­ed by Dun­ning and offer­ing a sober reminder of the human propen­si­ty for self-delu­sion. “We fre­quent­ly over­es­ti­mate our own abil­i­ties,” result­ing in wide­spread “illu­so­ry supe­ri­or­i­ty” that makes “incom­pe­tent peo­ple think they’re amaz­ing.” The effect great­ly inten­si­fies at the low­er end of the scale; it is often “those with the least abil­i­ty who are most like­ly to over­rate their skills to the great­est extent.” Or as Cleese plain­ly puts it, some peo­ple “are so stu­pid, they have no idea how stu­pid they are.”
Com­bine this with the con­verse effect—the ten­den­cy of skilled indi­vid­u­als to under­rate themselves—and we have the pre­con­di­tions for an epi­dem­ic of mis­matched skill sets and posi­tions. But while imposter syn­drome can pro­duce trag­ic per­son­al results and deprive the world of tal­ent, the Dun­ning-Kruger Effect’s worst casu­al­ties affect us all adverse­ly. Peo­ple “mea­sur­ably poor at log­i­cal rea­son­ing, gram­mar, finan­cial knowl­edge, math, emo­tion­al intel­li­gence, run­ning med­ical lab tests, and chess all tend to rate their exper­tise almost as favor­ably as actu­al experts do.” When such peo­ple get pro­mot­ed up the chain, they can unwit­ting­ly do a great deal of harm.
While arro­gant self-impor­tance plays its role in fos­ter­ing delu­sions of exper­tise, Dun­ning and Kruger found that most of us are sub­ject to the effect in some area of our lives sim­ply because we lack the skills to under­stand how bad we are at cer­tain things. We don’t know the rules well enough to suc­cess­ful­ly, cre­ative­ly break them. Until we have some basic under­stand­ing of what con­sti­tutes com­pe­tence in a par­tic­u­lar endeav­or, we can­not even under­stand that we’ve failed.
Real experts, on the oth­er hand, tend to assume their skills are ordi­nary and unre­mark­able. “The result is that peo­ple, whether they’re inept or high­ly skilled, are often caught in a bub­ble of inac­cu­rate self-per­cep­tion.” How can we get out? The answers won’t sur­prise you. Lis­ten to con­struc­tive feed­back and nev­er stop learn­ing, behav­ior that can require a good deal of vul­ner­a­bil­i­ty and humil­i­ty.
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2017.

title: Houston Center for Contemporary Craft Celebrates 25th Anniversary With Silver Exhibition
description: The most reflective element on Earth, silver has transformed the ways in which humans perceive, record, and understand the world. Presented on the
body:
The most reflective element on Earth, silver has transformed the ways in which humans perceive, record, and understand the world. Presented on the occasion of the Houston Center for Contemporary Craft’s milestone 25th anniversary, A Material Inheritance employs silver as both subject and lens, inviting reflection on the institution’s past while considering the evolving future of contemporary craft.
Silver is the material through which cultures have learned to see and remember themselves. Its exceptional optical and metallurgical properties made possible advances in mirror-making, photography, and scientific instrumentation, while its weight, density, and malleability established it as a prime medium for currency, ceremonial objects, jewelry, and treasured heirlooms. Looking beyond the material’s status as a precious metal, the exhibition considers how silver has shaped systems of knowledge, value, and cultural exchange across centuries and continents. 
Adam Whitney, “Unknown Echo,” (2023), fine silver .999, 24k gold gilding, garnet, display base, 7.5 x 4.5 x 9.75 inches (rhyton), 12.5 x 6.5 x 14.5 inches (with display base). Photo by Adam Whitney
Featuring artists Shane R. Hendren, Edward Lane McCartney, Jaydan Moore, Leah Ying Lin, Anjali Srinivasan, and others, A Material Inheritance presents works spanning traditional metalsmithing and jewelry making as well as experimental glass, ceramic, and kinetic media practices that reveal silver’s remarkable conceptual and material range. 
McCartney and Moore, who are alumni of Houston Center for Contemporary Craft’s Artist Residency Program, are metalsmiths whose practices are deeply intertwined with the history of the organization, and each offers a compelling investigation into inherited silver heirlooms, particularly domestic serving ware. Working from antique platters, teapots, flatware, and gifted family objects, both artists transform inherited silver from repositories of memory into dynamic sculptural forms, asking how objects accumulate meaning as they pass through generations.
Jaydan Moore, “TRACES #2,” (2025), found silver-plated platters, 44 x 35 x 9 inches. Photo by David Hunter Hale.
Across the works on view in A Material Inheritance, silver emerges as both substance and witness: a material shaped by histories of extraction, trade, migration, labor, and devotion, yet continually transformed through artistic experimentation. The exhibition positions silver as an active cultural agent that not only preserves histories but also continually refracts and reimagines them.
A Material Inheritance is on view through January 30, 2027, at the Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. Admission is free. 
Learn more at crafthouston.org. 
Anya Kivarkis, “Untitled” (brooch) (2005), ilver, enamel paint. Photo by Mike Bray

Installation view of “A Material Inheritance” at Houston Center for Contemporary Craft. Photo by Katy Anderson.

title: Art History and Pop Culture Converge in Friedrich Kunath's 'The Nearest Faraway Place'

body:
Friedrich Kunath describes that he aims to make his paintings “feel like songs.” The logo for the band Oasis turns up in a top corner of “Sometimes I’m Almost There,” and there is a kind of surreal, set-like quality to his vibrant, cinematic works. “Kunath explores themes of distance and (re)location, where a longing emerges between the place you’re in and the place you’re destined to be,” says a statement for his exhibition The Nearest Faraway Place, presented by Pace in Seoul.
The artist taps into art history with compositions redolent of the tradition of Weltlandschaft, or “the world landscape,” which can be traced to the Northern Renaissance. There’s also a strong nod to the Hudson River School, which drew on 19th-century European Romanticism. Kunath tips in references to pop culture, from the ubiquitous “The End” marking the finale of theatrical releases and phrases superimposed on uncanny situations, like the eponymous painting “The most beautiful world in the world” depicting an existential aerial advertisement.
“Sometimes I’m Almost There” (2026), oil on canvas, 121.9 x 97.8 centimeters
Kunath is known for traversing realms of pop culture, irony, and fiction, often with a kind of nostalgic wistfulness and a tinge of the comedic. We’re initially drawn in to what appears like a traditional landscape, then quickly diverted by sticker-like additions of cartoonish, sometimes absurd characters.
As the basis of the artist’s works, romantic landscapes are already inherently invented; they may resemble real places, but the glistening light and idyllic absence of structures or people portray a kind of ideal. Kunath opens that door further. “By bringing together aesthetic contexts and familiar tropes, he materializes his subconscious,” the gallery says. “Feelings arise before we know where they come from.”
The Nearest Faraway Place continues through October 24. See more on Kunath’s Instagram.

title: The Legacy of Colonialism Haunts Hew Locke's Era-Defying Flotilla

body:
Although Hew Locke’s practice revolves around geographically bound objects—superimposed drawings of Guyanese homes and his suspended flotilla among them—the artist traces the reaches of empire that extend far beyond any singular era or point on a map. How people, capital, cargo, and ideas traverse the globe has long been central to Locke’s work, an investigation he continues in The Wanderers on view at P·P·O·W.
Returning to the artist’s Odyssey series, the solo presentation hangs a fleet of miniature ships from the gallery ceiling. The flotilla features a wide array of boats, from tankers and fishing vessels to the towering galleons of the 16th century, which Locke embellishes with tiny pennants strung between the masts, foliage springing from the sides, and coats of colorful paint that appear as vibrantly aged patina. Referencing the global history of trade and exploitation, the ships all journey together toward un undetermined future, the legacy of their pasts in tow.
“Souvenir 28 (Victoria)” (2025), mixed media on antique Parian ware, 22 1/4 x 6 1/8 x 5 3/4 inches. Photo by Damian Griffiths
Conquest and the desire for control and wealth also appear in Locke’s lavish busts, which adorn Parian ware (a porcelain that emerged in the mid-19th century as an economical dupe for marble) with a trove of glittering baubles. Titled as Souvenirs, these mixed-media sculptures depict figures like Queen Victoria and George Washington and revel in artifice and ostentatious displays of power that soar high in the air. 
Several skeletons are embedded within the costuming, gesturing toward memento mori and implicating these powerhouses in the afterlives of their colonial projects. The figures appear haunted by death and, as Locke says, are “weighed down by the literal burden of history.” 
The Wanderers is on view through October 24 in New York. Find more from Locke on Instagram.
